blocks.text: A 68-year-old woman is found on the kitchen floor with a right-sided facial droop and slurred speech. The paramedics note that she last spoke normally 90 minutes earlier. Before anything else is decided, a non-contrast CT of the head must answer one question in a few minutes: is there blood in the brain?

blocks.markdown: **CT is the first test for the brain in an emergency.** It is fast, widely available and shows acute blood clearly. Fresh blood is denser than brain tissue, so acute haemorrhage appears **hyperdense** (bright). Over days to weeks it becomes isodense and then hypodense as it breaks down, which helps date a collection. An **infarct** is initially subtle, because the first CT may look normal for hours. Early signs include loss of the normal grey-white differentiation (such as the insular ribbon), sulcal effacement and a dense (bright) artery within the vessel; later the infarct becomes **hypodense** (dark) as water accumulates. Haemorrhage must be excluded before thrombolysis, and CT angiography or perfusion imaging can identify an occluded vessel for thrombectomy. MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is more sensitive for early infarcts and for small posterior circulation strokes but is slower and less available.

rows: Biconvex (lens-shaped) bright collection that does not cross sutures
Head injury with temporal bone fracture and tear of the middle meningeal artery
Crescentic bright collection that crosses sutures but not the midline dural folds
Tearing of bridging veins, older adults, alcohol, anticoagulants
Can be acute, subacute or chronic with changing density
Blood in the basal cisterns, sulci or fissures
Thunderclap headache; CT very sensitive early, less sensitive after several days
Bright rounded or irregular parenchymal collection
May cause mass effect and midline shift
blocks.caption: Patterns of intracranial haemorrhage on CT.

ABC/2 method for estimating the volume of an intracerebral haematoma: A is the largest diameter on the slice with the biggest area, B is the largest diameter perpendicular to A on that slice, and C is the vertical extent (number of slices containing the bleed multiplied by slice thickness), all in centimetres, giving volume in cubic centimetres (equal to millilitres).

blocks.title: Estimating a haematoma volume
blocks.prompt: On CT a woman has an intracerebral haemorrhage. On the largest slice the haematoma measures 5.0 cm by 3.2 cm, and it is visible on 8 consecutive 5 mm slices. Estimate its volume.

steps.text: Convert slice thickness. 5 mm is 0.5 cm, so the vertical extent C = 8 x 0.5 cm = 4.0 cm.
Apply the formula. V = A x B x C / 2 = 5.0 x 3.2 x 4.0 / 2 cm^3.

Interpret. The ABC/2 method treats the bleed as an ellipsoid, so it approximates irregular haematomas. Volume, location and signs such as midline shift or intraventricular extension help predict outcome and guide neurosurgical discussion.

blocks.answer: The estimated volume is about 32 mL, an approximation that is used together with location and clinical status.

blocks.title: Haemorrhage versus infarct on the first CT
blocks.text: On a non-contrast CT, bright means acute blood and dark means older infarct or oedema. A normal early CT does not exclude infarct, so treatment decisions rest on the clinical picture and CT is mainly used to exclude haemorrhage and other mimics. Always search for a dense vessel, loss of grey-white differentiation and sulcal effacement.

blocks.markdown: **Describing a fracture.** A radiograph should be requested in at least two projections at right angles, and include the joints above and below the injury for long bones. Describe a fracture systematically: *which bone and where* (proximal, shaft, distal; extra-articular or intra-articular); the *pattern* (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, impacted or avulsion); *displacement and angulation* (translation, the direction in which the distal fragment points, and rotation); *associated features* (joint dislocation, soft tissue swelling, an open wound which makes the fracture open rather than closed); and any underlying bone abnormality. In children, growth plate injuries are classified by the **Salter-Harris** system, where type I passes through the physis, type II through the physis and metaphysis, type III through the physis and epiphysis, type IV through all three, and type V is a crush injury of the physis.

rows: Distal radius, 2.5 cm from the joint line
Swelling, gas, foreign body, open wound
blocks.caption: A systematic description of a fracture on a radiograph.

blocks.title: Describing a wrist radiograph
blocks.prompt: A 72-year-old woman falls onto an outstretched hand. The radiograph shows a transverse fracture of the distal radius 2.5 cm proximal to the wrist joint with 20 degrees of dorsal angulation. The joint surface is intact and the bones appear osteopenic. How do you describe this?

steps.text: Identify bone and site. Distal radius, extra-articular, about 2.5 cm from the joint.
Describe pattern and displacement. Transverse, with dorsal angulation of the distal fragment of about 20 degrees.
Note joint and bone quality. The articular surface is not involved and the bones look osteopenic, supporting a fragility fracture.

Summarise and act. This is a closed dorsally angulated extra-articular distal radial fracture (a Colles-type fracture). The osteopenia prompts bone health assessment and falls review, and the orthopaedic team decides on reduction and immobilisation.

blocks.answer: A closed, dorsally angulated, extra-articular distal radial fracture in osteopenic bone, needing orthopaedic management and fragility assessment.

blocks.markdown: **Common bone pathology on radiographs.** A **fragility fracture** of a vertebra shows loss of vertebral body height, often anteriorly or centrally, and general osteopenia. The percentage height loss is $(h_{normal}-h_{fractured})/h_{normal}\times100$ and is used to grade severity. A **pathological fracture** occurs through abnormal bone: look for a lytic (dark) or sclerotic (dense) lesion, cortical destruction, an aggressive periosteal reaction and a wide zone of transition. Osteomyelitis may show osteopenia, periosteal reaction and later bone destruction, and radiographs lag behind disease by days to weeks. Some fractures, such as scaphoid, can be invisible on the first radiograph, so persistent anatomical snuffbox tenderness warrants immobilisation with repeat imaging or MRI.

**Suspected spinal cord compression.** Cord compression is an emergency because delay in decompression leads to irreversible paralysis. Red flags include new back or neck pain (especially at night or thoracic), progressive limb weakness, a sensory level, bladder or bowel dysfunction, and a background of cancer. Cauda equina compression below the conus produces saddle anaesthesia, bladder and bowel dysfunction and lower motor neuron signs in the legs. **MRI** of the whole spine is the investigation of choice because it shows the cord, thecal sac, vertebral marrow and soft tissue, and it should be arranged urgently, usually within 24 hours for suspected malignant cord compression with neurological features, as set out in current NICE guidance. Plain radiographs are insensitive and should not delay MRI. CT or CT myelography is used when MRI is contraindicated or unavailable.

blocks.title: Choosing imaging for new weakness in a patient with cancer
blocks.prompt: A 64-year-old man with known prostate cancer has had 3 weeks of progressive thoracic back pain, worse at night. This morning both legs feel weak, he has a sensory level at the umbilicus and cannot pass urine. What imaging do you request and why?

steps.text: Recognise the syndrome. Back pain with bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level and urinary retention in a patient with cancer indicates metastatic spinal cord compression until proved otherwise.
Choose the test. MRI of the whole spine is required because it shows the level and degree of cord compression and detects further sites of disease, since multiple levels are common.
Avoid delaying the test. A plain radiograph would be insensitive and would waste time, so the request is made urgently as an emergency with a senior clinician informed.
Plan what follows. The result guides decisions by the oncology and spinal surgical teams, including radiotherapy or surgery; early referral and bladder and neurological monitoring are part of care.

blocks.answer: Urgent MRI of the whole spine, because it best shows cord compression and other levels, with the oncology and spinal teams alerted immediately.

blocks.title: Do not reassure on a plain film or delay MRI
blocks.text: A normal spine radiograph does not exclude cord or cauda equina compression, and bony metastases may be invisible until a large part of the trabecular bone is destroyed. New neurological signs with back pain need urgent MRI and senior input, not repeated observation or a wait for routine imaging.

points: Non-contrast CT head is the first test in suspected stroke or head injury; acute blood is bright, infarct is subtle early and dark later; know the shapes of extradural, subdural and subarachnoid bleeds.
Intracerebral haematoma volume can be estimated as ABC/2.
Describe a fracture by site, pattern, alignment, joint involvement, soft tissue and cause; Salter-Harris classifies growth plate injuries.
Look for lytic or sclerotic lesions in pathological fractures and be aware that an occult fracture such as scaphoid may not show on the first film.
Suspected spinal cord compression needs urgent whole spine MRI rather than plain films.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man on warfarin fell 2 weeks ago and is now drowsy. A non-contrast CT shows a crescent-shaped collection over the left cerebral hemisphere that crosses suture lines and is slightly brighter than brain. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.text: Subarachnoid haemorrhage in the basal cisterns

distractorRationale.a: Extradural collections are lens-shaped and do not cross sutures.
distractorRationale.b: An infarct is dark and wedge-shaped, not a bright extra-axial collection.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: crescentic, crosses sutures, in an older anticoagulated patient after a fall.
distractorRationale.d: Subarachnoid blood lies in the cisterns and sulci, not as a crescent over the hemisphere.

questions.explanation: A crescentic extra-axial collection that crosses suture lines and is bounded by dural folds is subdural, and it is common in older patients and those on anticoagulants because bridging veins tear. Extradural bleeds are biconvex and follow arterial injury.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old boy falls from a bicycle. The radiograph shows a fracture line passing through the growth plate and out through the metaphysis, leaving a triangle of metaphysis attached to the epiphysis. Which Salter-Harris type is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: through the physis and metaphysis is type II.
distractorRationale.b: Type I passes through the physis alone.
distractorRationale.c: Type III passes through the physis and epiphysis.
distractorRationale.d: Type V is a crush injury of the physis.

questions.explanation: In Salter-Harris type II, the fracture runs along the physis and exits through the metaphysis. Recognising the type matters because growth plate involvement can affect later growth.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand and has pain in the anatomical snuffbox. The initial wrist radiographs look normal. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
Order a CT of the head
Treat as a suspected scaphoid fracture with immobilisation and further imaging such as MRI or repeat radiographs

questions.correctOptionText: Treat as a suspected scaphoid fracture with immobilisation and further imaging such as MRI or repeat radiographs

distractorRationale.a: Normal radiographs do not exclude scaphoid fracture.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: scaphoid fractures can be occult at first and a missed fracture risks nonunion and avascular necrosis.

questions.explanation: Scaphoid fractures are often invisible on the first radiograph, and delayed diagnosis risks nonunion and avascular necrosis of the proximal pole. Clinical suspicion therefore justifies immobilisation and further imaging, per local protocol.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with breast cancer has 2 weeks of progressive mid-back pain and new difficulty climbing stairs. Examination shows brisk leg reflexes and a sensory level. Which investigation is most appropriate?

options.text: Urgent MRI of the whole spine

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent MRI of the whole spine

distractorRationale.a: Plain films are insensitive and may be falsely reassuring.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: MRI shows cord compression and multiple levels of disease.
distractorRationale.c: A chest radiograph does not evaluate the cord.
distractorRationale.d: Ultrasound cannot image through the bony spinal canal in adults.

questions.explanation: A sensory level, brisk reflexes and leg weakness in a patient with cancer indicate suspected metastatic cord compression, which needs urgent whole spine MRI. Delay risks permanent paralysis.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has sudden weakness of the left arm and leg. A non-contrast CT performed 1 hour after onset is reported as normal. What does this mean?

options.text: It proves a transient ischaemic attack
It excludes haemorrhage but does not exclude an early infarct
It shows the stroke is old

questions.correctOptionText: It excludes haemorrhage but does not exclude an early infarct

distractorRationale.a: Early infarcts are frequently invisible on CT.
distractorRationale.b: A normal CT does not distinguish TIA from stroke.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: CT is sensitive for blood but often normal in the first hours of infarct.
distractorRationale.d: No imaging feature here suggests an old stroke.

questions.explanation: CT demonstrates acute blood well but may not yet show the hypodensity of infarction in the first hours. A normal early CT therefore removes haemorrhage as a cause and treatment decisions rest on the clinical presentation, with further vascular imaging as needed.

questions.stem: On CT an intracerebral haematoma measures 4.0 cm by 3.0 cm on the largest slice and appears on 6 slices each 5 mm thick. Using the ABC/2 method, estimate the volume in mL.
questions.explanation: Vertical extent C = 6 x 0.5 cm = 3.0 cm, so V = 4.0 x 3.0 x 3.0 / 2 = 36 / 2 = 18 cm^3, which equals 18 mL. The ABC/2 method assumes an ellipsoid, so it is an estimate for irregular bleeds.

questions.stem: A normal vertebral body height is 24 mm. A fragility fracture reduces the measured anterior height to 16 mm. Calculate the percentage loss of vertebral height.
questions.explanation: Percentage loss = (24 - 16) / 24 x 100 = 8 / 24 x 100 = 33.3%. Height loss is used to grade vertebral fractures and to document progression, which should lead to assessment of bone health.

questions.stem: Compare the CT appearances of acute intracranial haemorrhage and early ischaemic infarct, and explain why CT is used first in suspected stroke.
markingGuide: Acute blood is hyperdense (bright); extradural is biconvex, subdural crescentic, subarachnoid in cisterns
Early infarct may be normal; signs include loss of grey-white differentiation, sulcal effacement, dense vessel
CT is fast and available and excludes haemorrhage before thrombolysis
MRI diffusion is more sensitive but slower
CT angiography identifies large vessel occlusion
questions.explanation: Haemorrhage is easily seen on CT but infarct is initially subtle, which is why CT is used mainly to exclude blood and to guide time-critical treatment. Further imaging refines the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Describe how you would report a long bone fracture on a radiograph and list features that suggest a pathological rather than a traumatic fracture.
markingGuide: Two views including joint above and below
Intra- or extra-articular, dislocation, open or closed, soft tissue
Pathological features: lytic or sclerotic lesion, cortical destruction, aggressive periosteal reaction, wide zone of transition, minimal trauma
Recommend further imaging or referral where appropriate
questions.explanation: A structured description conveys the information required for management and avoids missed features. Findings of underlying bone lesions change management from simple fracture care to investigation of the lesion.

questions.stem: A patient presents with back pain and bilateral leg weakness. Explain how you would select imaging for suspected spinal cord compression, why plain radiographs are inadequate, and what clinical features help to distinguish cord from cauda equina compression.
markingGuide: Urgent MRI whole spine, usually within 24 hours for suspected malignant cord compression per NICE
Shows cord, canal, marrow, soft tissue and multiple levels
Plain films insensitive and should not delay MRI
CT or CT myelography if MRI contraindicated
Cord: upper motor neuron signs, sensory level
Cauda equina: saddle anaesthesia, lower motor neuron signs, bladder and bowel dysfunction
Emergency referral to spinal or oncology team
questions.explanation: Compression needs urgent MRI because it shows the cause and extent and prevents irreversible loss of function. The pattern of signs helps to localise the lesion and communicate the urgency.
